Chapter 5: Creating a New Relationship with Time and Focus.
As you keep moving forward on your path to a more fulfilling life, there’s another powerful shift to make—rethinking how you see time.
I mean, have you ever felt completely boxed in by your schedule? Like you’re racing against the clock, always behind, and there’s just never enough time for the things that matter most?
If you’re nodding, you’re not alone. This kind of thinking brings on stress and distraction—and it feeds that nagging feeling that you’re always playing catch-up. It’s actually one of the ways we keep ourselves stuck, by making it so hard to focus on what truly matters.
But what if you could flip the script? What if, instead of being at the mercy of time, you could actually be in charge of it?
There’s a whole new way to look at this. It’s called “Einstein Time.” Instead of letting the clock control you, you start relating to time with presence, with real choice, and even with creativity.
Here’s the big idea: Time isn’t some outside force that rules your life. It’s a resource you get to shape and direct. When you’re truly present—when your mind’s right here, engaged—time almost feels like it expands. But when you’re distracted, or resisting what’s in front of you, time just shrinks and gets tense.
So, how do you actually start building this new relationship with time? Here are a few practical steps:
First, start by taking ownership. Instead of saying, “I don’t have time,” try saying, “I’m choosing how to spend my time.” That shift puts you back in the driver’s seat, making conscious decisions about what matters.
Next, focus on what’s most important to you—especially those activities that light you up and really align with your Zone of Genius. Prioritize those, and let go of the stuff that just drains your energy or doesn’t move you toward your core goals.
Another key? Be fully present. Whether you’re working, spending time with someone, or just enjoying a quiet moment, give it your full attention. Forget multitasking or worrying about what’s next. When you do, you’ll not only get more done—you’ll actually enjoy it a whole lot more.
And here’s something else to notice: Any time you catch yourself believing there’s just not enough time, try experimenting with the idea that time can actually be abundant and flexible. It takes practice, but it’s a game-changer.
Think of time like a river you can navigate, not a treadmill you’re stuck running on. When you choose where to focus your energy, you start moving with the current, instead of fighting against it.
This new way of relating to time isn’t just about getting more done—it’s about creating space for creativity, for connection, and for what really matters to you.
So, as you start weaving these practices into your day, you’ll find it’s possible to break free from those old limits. You’ll live with more ease, with real purpose, and with a deeper sense of joy.
